title: Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact
subtitle: Public peace, secret partition, and the decision to cooperate
author: Robert M. Dobo
summary: Germany and the Soviet Union promised nonaggression while secretly assigning spheres of influence across eastern Europe. Diplomatic records reveal the choices, deadlines, and territorial concessions behind a bargain that facilitated Germany’s attack on Poland.

asides.label: Stalin was present. He did not sign.

body:
In Moscow on August 23, 1939, Joachim von Ribbentrop and Vyacheslav Molotov negotiated a public treaty and a secret territorial bargain. Their public treaty promised ten years of peaceful relations between Germany and the Soviet Union. The secret protocol left Poland’s continued independence for their governments to decide. The treaty promised restraint between the two powers; the protocol treated their neighbours’ territory as something they could bargain over. Poland had no representative in the room. Berlin and Moscow reserved that decision for themselves. [1] [2] The agreement exposed a possibility that ideological hostility had obscured. Hitler’s regime and Stalin’s regime could cooperate when each expected to gain by allowing the other freedom of action. Ribbentrop brought authority to conclude the bargain quickly; Molotov negotiated with Stalin present and exercising decisive political authority. Their accommodation did not require reconciliation between Nazism and communism. Each government weighed immediate gains against risks, at the expense of other states’ independence. [3] [4] The documents bore the date August 23, although negotiation and signing continued into the early hours of August 24. American ambassador Laurence Steinhardt reported that morning that Molotov and Ribbentrop had signed in the Kremlin and that Stalin had attended the final conference. The familiar date is the date placed on the instruments, not a claim that the business ended before midnight. Germany invaded Poland nine days after that dated agreement. [4] a The urgency of those nine days should not erase the preceding choices. German planning for an attack already existed; Moscow had also been negotiating with Britain and France. The issue is how those possibilities narrowed into a bargain that improved Germany’s immediate position and offered the Soviet leadership a territorial opportunity. This study follows that decision and its immediate diplomatic aftermath. The invasions and the revised September partition required further decisions, examined in the studies that follow.

An unsettled Europe

Poland had recovered independence in 1918 after more than a century of partition, but its eastern frontier emerged from another war. The Treaty of Riga, signed on March 18, 1921, ended the Polish–Soviet conflict and established the boundary that remained in place in 1939. It was registered with the League of Nations; Britain, France, and Italy recognized the frontier in March 1923. Recognition did not mean those governments guaranteed its inviolability. Historian Mariusz Wołos emphasizes that distinction: Poland possessed an internationally recognized frontier while remaining vulnerable to the powers that disputed the settlement. [5] The Riga settlement also remained part of the legal relationship between Warsaw and Moscow. Polish diplomacy referred to it in the nonaggression pact concluded with the Soviet Union in 1932. The dispute in 1939 therefore concerned a state with existing treaty relations, rather than an unallocated borderland. Its eastern provinces contained Polish, Ukrainian, Belarusian, and Jewish communities, among others. Their diverse attachments could not be reduced to the territorial preferences of Berlin or Moscow. Recognition of that diversity requires attention to the inhabitants; it does not confer a right upon foreign governments to dispose of them. [5] [6] b Germany and Soviet Russia had cooperated before, under different circumstances. At Rapallo in 1922, Weimar Germany and Soviet Russia restored diplomatic relations and renounced specified claims against one another, including claims arising from the war. The Berlin Treaty of 1926 maintained that relationship and promised neutrality if one party was attacked despite its peaceful conduct. Both governments sought relief from isolation. This history supplied an established language of friendship and mutual advantage to which the 1939 treaty explicitly appealed. It did not make the later territorial bargain inevitable: the regimes, their ambitions, and the commitments they were now prepared to undertake had changed. [7] [8] [1] c Hitler’s accession to power in 1933 fundamentally changed the character of German policy. Nazi hostility to communism was bound up with a racial vision of conquest. The idea of Lebensraum envisaged expansion into eastern Europe, German settlement and the displacement or subordination of peoples the regime considered inferior. It gave the German–Soviet confrontation an importance that went far beyond an ordinary disagreement between states. An agreement with Stalin could serve Hitler’s immediate purposes without ending those longer ambitions. [9] d The sequence of German advances narrowed the room for compromise. Rearmament and the remilitarization of the Rhineland were followed by the annexation of Austria in March 1938. [10] Later that year, the crisis over Czechoslovakia brought Britain and France to Munich. On September 29–30, their leaders joined Germany and Italy in accepting the transfer of the Sudetenland. Czechoslovakia was excluded from the conference that determined its territorial losses. [11] The exclusion of the Soviet Union from Munich strengthened the grounds on which Moscow could question Western policy, although it does not by itself establish Stalin’s subsequent intentions. German occupation of the Czech lands in March 1939 demonstrated that territorial concessions had failed to contain Hitler’s ambitions. London and Paris consequently had to reconsider how a commitment to resist further expansion could be made credible. Their difficulty was simultaneously political and military: announcing a limit to concessions was easier than assembling the forces and agreements required to enforce it. [12] e

Poland between two powers

German pressure now centred on Poland. Hitler’s government wanted the Free City of Danzig, today Gdańsk, incorporated into Germany and sought an extraterritorial transport connection through the Polish Corridor. The language of roads and territorial adjustments understated the political stakes. Accepting German demands risked making Polish independence increasingly dependent on Berlin’s goodwill; refusing them exposed Poland to a stronger neighbour already willing to use force. The British guarantee of Polish independence on March 31, 1939, together with France’s existing commitment, sought to increase the prospective cost of a German attack. Its credibility nevertheless depended on a practical question: how quickly could the Western powers exert pressure sufficient to help Poland? Their geographical position made Soviet policy central to that calculation, because the Soviet Union could threaten Germany from the east while Britain and France faced it from the west. Diplomatic commitment and operational assistance would have to be connected for the guarantee to achieve its purpose. [13] German planning did not wait for an agreement with Moscow. On April 3, Hitler issued instructions for Fall Weiss, the operation against Poland, with preparations allowing an attack from the beginning of September. On April 28, he renounced Germany’s existing nonaggression arrangement with Poland. The sequence is essential: the August pact facilitated an aggressive policy that was already taking shape. It did not suddenly create Germany’s interest in attacking its neighbour. [13] [12] [27] f For Warsaw, the question of allowing Soviet troops to cross Polish territory made security and sovereignty inseparable. Soviet forces could not engage Germany across a common German–Soviet frontier, because none existed. They would need access through another country. Polish leaders had to consider whether troops admitted as assistance would leave when the emergency ended. Britain and France could urge cooperation, but they could not grant passage through Poland on its government’s behalf. The problem was real even before either side used it to assign blame for the breakdown of negotiations. [14] A military convention therefore required more than agreement that German aggression was dangerous. It needed routes, consent, and a credible relationship among governments that distrusted one another. Polish refusal narrowed the practical possibilities for a coalition, while Soviet insistence placed a condition on assistance that Warsaw feared could destroy the independence it was intended to defend. Neither fact establishes that a German–Soviet territorial bargain was the only possible response. The failure of one negotiation and the decision to partition other states remain separate questions of responsibility. [15] [14] g

The diplomatic choice

During the 1930s, Soviet diplomacy had pursued collective security against aggression. Maxim Litvinov, the foreign commissar closely associated with cooperation with the Western powers, was replaced by Molotov on May 3, 1939. In retrospect, the appointment can look like the first decisive step toward the pact. Contemporaries did not agree about what it meant. American diplomatic reporting on May 4 preserved several contemporary interpretations of Litvinov’s dismissal. The Soviet ambassador in Paris denied that it signaled a policy change, while Józef Beck reportedly anticipated a change in methods more than objectives; French assessments were cautious as well. These responses reveal the uncertainty in which diplomacy proceeded. They support a history of choices being assessed and revised during the spring, rather than an inference that every change of personnel already contained the outcome reached in August. [16] By August, Britain, France, and the Soviet Union were discussing military cooperation, and transit remained an obstacle. On August 23, Steinhardt reported that the French ambassador assigned principal responsibility for the delay to Poland’s refusal of Soviet military assistance. Steinhardt added his own, different judgment: Polish agreement at that point probably would no longer prevent a German–Soviet accord. The distinction matters. A participant was explaining failure by blaming Warsaw; an outside observer was questioning whether the alternative still existed. Neither dispatch can reveal the precise moment when Stalin decided against the Western negotiations. [15] The British account recorded an acrimonious encounter. Molotov accused the British and French military missions of arriving without an answer to the passage question. Ambassador Sir William Seeds denied that they could dispose of a third country’s territory. He also pressed Molotov on the effect of a German agreement: would Moscow stand aside while Poland was overrun? Molotov declined to give a definite answer. The exchange, relayed through Halifax to American ambassador Joseph Kennedy, documents the rupture in confidence as well as the military impasse. It is a chain of diplomatic reporting, not a transcript of the Soviet leadership’s private deliberations. [14] h Berlin could offer Moscow advantages that a defensive coalition could not legitimately offer: recognition of Soviet interests in other states’ territory, negotiated without their consent. Germany sought freedom to attack Poland without Soviet opposition. Stalin obtained German acceptance of a Soviet sphere and an opportunity to remain outside the opening German conflict with the Western powers. The advantages were complementary without being identical. Hitler wanted an immediate obstacle removed; Stalin could bargain over the territorial and political terms on which it would be removed. [2] [3] How long Stalin expected this relationship to last remains a question of interpretation. In a published interview about Stalin’s Wars, historian Geoffrey Roberts said that his research had made him more inclined to think Stalin contemplated a long-term alliance, at least until relations deteriorated in the summer of 1940. That is Roberts’s assessment of intended duration, rather than a conclusion contained in the August protocol. The protocol establishes something more immediate: Soviet leaders negotiated territorial opportunities as part of the agreement. Security calculations and expansion could coexist. Explaining the first does not remove responsibility for the second. [17] [2] i Economic negotiation had helped make the political approach possible. The commercial agreement of August 19 provided a German credit of 200 million Reichsmarks for Soviet industrial purchases, to be repaid through raw-material deliveries. Karl Schnurre’s memorandum of August 29 distinguished this credit from additional current trade, under which Soviet raw materials and German manufactured goods would be exchanged. Machinery and industrial installations figured prominently among Soviet purchases. Germany wanted supplies with immediate wartime value. Schnurre explicitly described the talks as a means of renewing political contacts: commercial obligations provided a practical reason for officials to keep dealing with one another while relations were being transformed. [18] j Hitler’s personal message to Stalin on August 20 imposed a much shorter horizon. He accepted the Soviet draft of the nonaggression treaty, requested Ribbentrop’s reception on August 22 or 23, and said that the foreign minister could remain for no more than one or two days. Ribbentrop would have authority to sign both the treaty and the supplementary protocol. Hitler blamed intolerable tension on Poland, but the operationally useful information in his message was the deadline: he wanted the Soviet answer before proceeding with a crisis his own government was preparing to turn into war. [3] Stalin answered on August 21, agreeing to receive Ribbentrop on the 23rd. His reply expressed the hope that the agreement would improve relations between the two states. Behind the conventional language lay a rapid transformation. While other governments were still trying to understand Moscow’s intentions, the German foreign minister was preparing to conclude a bargain at the highest level. [19] k

A night in Moscow

Ribbentrop’s authority did not settle every demand in advance. After three hours with Stalin and Molotov on August 23, he reported that agreement depended on German recognition that the Latvian ports of Libau and Windau, now Liepāja and Ventspils, lay within the proposed Soviet sphere of influence. He asked Berlin to obtain Hitler’s assent. Both ports lay in independent Latvia. Germany was being asked to recognize a Soviet sphere within Latvia without consulting the Latvian government. [20] Berlin approved. The published records identify telephone transmission, with the answer received in Moscow at 11 p.m. Such a brief exchange could dispose of a major objection because Latvia’s consent was never a condition of agreement. The negotiators were drawing limits on one another’s prospective action. They could agree rapidly precisely because the interests of the countries named in the protocol were not represented as independent claims requiring settlement. [21] l The German diplomat Hencke’s memorandum records how the participants justified the reversal to one another. Ribbentrop represented the Anti-Comintern Pact, formally directed against communist influence, as chiefly aimed against the Western democracies. Stalin and Molotov joined him in criticizing Britain, while Stalin also warned that Britain would fight stubbornly. Ceremonial toasts, including Stalin’s toast to Hitler, accompanied the discussion. These were recorded diplomatic statements, shaped by the occasion and the German recorder; they reveal the language used to build cooperation without granting direct access to every participant’s beliefs. [22] The memorandum also exposes a tension in Ribbentrop’s presentation. He claimed that Germans warmly welcomed friendship with the Soviet Union. Stalin attributed that welcome to a desire for peace; Ribbentrop agreed, then insisted that every man was ready to fight Poland. Both assertions served his negotiating position. They are not evidence of unanimous German opinion. The juxtaposition explains the practical meaning of the peace being celebrated: restraint between Berlin and Moscow could coexist with preparations to attack a neighbour, and the foreign minister could present the two purposes as entirely compatible. [22] m

Two documents, two audiences

The public treaty contained seven articles. Germany and the Soviet Union promised to refrain from aggression against one another, maintain consultation, settle disputes peacefully, and avoid groupings directed against the other party. Article II withheld support from a third power engaged in belligerent action against either signatory. These commitments restricted the coalition options open to both governments. The consequences for Poland lay in that restriction: Soviet cooperation with Britain and France against Germany would now collide with undertakings Moscow had just made to Berlin. [1] Its projected duration was ten years, with an automatic extension of five years unless notice of termination was given in advance. Ratification was to follow, but the treaty entered into force immediately upon signature. The legal form suggested continuity and stability at precisely the moment when the strategic relationship had changed with extraordinary speed. [1] The wording weakened an earlier safeguard. The Berlin Treaty of 1926 had promised neutrality when a party was attacked despite its peaceful conduct. The 1939 pact invoked that treaty in its preamble but supplied no explicit escape clause if a signatory itself attacked a third country. Seeds had asked Molotov about precisely such a provision before the signing and received no assurance. The difference was consequential: a bilateral promise of nonassistance could shelter an aggressor from intervention by the other signatory. Poland’s danger lay in the commitments Germany had secured, not simply in the public language of reconciliation. [8] [1] [14] n

Made public

A nonaggression treaty

Promises governing relations between Germany and the Soviet Union. Ten-year term; effective on signature.

Kept secret

A division of interests

Proposed spheres across eastern Europe, negotiated without the affected states’ consent.

The secret protocol addressed those third countries directly. Under the formula of a possible “territorial and political rearrangement,” it divided German and Soviet interests across a broad region. Finland, Estonia and Latvia fell within the Soviet sphere. Lithuania was initially on the German side, with the northern Lithuanian frontier serving as the dividing line between the two spheres. The document also recognized Lithuania’s interest in the Vilna region, including the city then within Poland and now known as Vilnius. [2] For Poland, the protocol proposed an approximate division along the Narew, Vistula and San rivers. It left open whether an independent Polish state would survive and what its frontiers might be. Those questions were to be settled by subsequent agreement between Berlin and Moscow. The uncertainty was itself revealing: the signatories treated the continued existence of a neighbouring sovereign state as a matter for their own convenience. In southeastern Europe, the Soviet side emphasized its interest in Bessarabia, then part of Romania, while Germany declared political disinterest in that territory. The protocol thus extended well beyond Poland. It offered a framework in which German and Soviet ambitions could proceed without immediate conflict with each other. [2] The August text left two kinds of uncertainty. Its territorial division was approximate, and the survival of a reduced Poland was conditional on the signatories’ interests. Neither uncertainty preserved Polish authority over the decision. Both made further bargaining necessary. The September agreement would alter the division and settle the question differently, showing how the partners continued to trade advantages after their armies entered Poland. [2] The protocol supplied no invasion timetable or common operational command. It also transferred no lawful sovereignty. Its river line recorded a diplomatic allocation, not the location of soldiers or administrations on August 23. Reading it that way preserves the difference between agreeing to permit expansion and carrying it out: the invasions remained actions for which governments and commanders would issue further instructions. [2] o

Names on the document

Stalin was present. He did not sign.

The signatures belonged to Molotov and Ribbentrop. Stalin’s presence and political authority were central to the negotiations, but his name was not one of the treaty’s signatures. The alternative name “Hitler–Stalin Pact” identifies the leaders responsible for the bargain; “Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact” identifies its signatories. p

[1] [4]

What the world could see

The announcement transformed the diplomatic situation before most governments could discover the territorial terms. British reports recorded suspicion of a new partition, but suspicion was different from possession of the secret protocol. For London and Paris, the immediate problem was whether an agreement intended to isolate Poland would also discourage them from resisting Germany. For Warsaw, the danger was that the collapse of the hoped-for coalition would leave an alliance on paper without a practicable means of delivering help. [14] Britain’s response included making its commitment more formal. On August 25, London and Warsaw signed their Agreement of Mutual Assistance. Its public text promised help if either party became involved in hostilities through aggression by a European power, and also addressed threats to independence that compelled armed resistance. This was a warning that a German–Soviet arrangement had not removed the prospect of British belligerency. It supplied no immediate solution to the geographical difficulty of assisting Poland. [23] Polish diplomacy, meanwhile, continued to present willingness to negotiate without surrendering independence. In his reply to President Franklin Roosevelt on August 25, President Ignacy Mościcki said that Poland was ready for direct discussions and procedures of conciliation; he also emphasized that Poland was making no territorial demands. This was an official Polish representation of its position, intended to influence American and wider opinion. It matters because the surviving record includes an attempt to avert war alongside the preparations to resist it. Roosevelt’s appeal was diplomatic intervention by a country that had made no commitment to fight for Poland. [24] q The alliance and Italy’s position temporarily complicated Hitler’s timetable. The postwar International Military Tribunal’s reconstruction, based on captured German documents, identified both the Anglo-Polish agreement and Mussolini’s unwillingness to enter an immediate war as factors in the postponement of the attack planned for August 26. Daladier also appealed directly to Hitler on August 26. These developments did not reverse German policy, but the postponement demonstrates that the decision in Moscow had not settled the decisions in London, Paris or Rome. Germany still faced a choice about accepting the risk of a wider war. [25] r The agreement also unsettled Germany’s relationships farther afield. Japan, a partner in the Anti-Comintern Pact, was fighting Soviet forces at Khalkhin Gol, also known as Nomonhan, during the same summer. Tokyo’s struggle with Moscow gave the German reversal an immediate strategic meaning. A government associated with opposition to international communism had reached an accommodation with the Soviet Union while Japanese troops were engaged against it. [26] s

The decision that remained

By the end of August, the pact had improved the conditions for an attack without eliminating its risks. Britain formalized its commitment to Poland, Italy withheld immediate participation, and Hitler temporarily postponed the offensive. These were consequential decisions by other governments, not minor interruptions in an inevitable sequence. The German leadership still had to choose whether to attack in circumstances that might bring a European war. The Soviet government had chosen to facilitate German freedom of action while securing territorial opportunities of its own. [25] [2] t Poland still possessed its territory, government, and armed forces. The secret protocol had placed its future on a negotiating table; it had not yet imposed the outcome on its inhabitants. Turning the bargain into control would require the use of force against a state still able to resist. The study of September 1 follows the decision into the crossings, frontier positions, and roads where Germany’s diplomatic advantage had to become military power. [12]
sourceMethod: Numbered citations identify the passages used and link back to their first appearance. The public treaty and secret protocol are read separately, alongside dated German and American diplomatic correspondence. Published English transcriptions and translations were consulted, including retained full-text source copies; original manuscripts were not inspected. Diplomatic reports establish what officials reported, not an unmediated account of Stalin’s intentions or popular opinion. Roberts’s argument is cited to his accessible interview, not to an uninspected copy of his book. The narrative distinguishes evidence from interpretation and ends with the decisions immediately preceding the invasion.
